title: Sorted input sinks quicksort
hook: Hand it cards already in order. Does it get the easy job?

knows: partitioning around a pivot: smaller cards go one side, bigger the other (quicksort-partition)
doesNotKnow: that the pivot rule decides the cost
that an already sorted list is the worst case when the first card is the pivot

misconception: An already sorted list is the easiest thing to sort.
objective: The learner can explain that with the first card as pivot, a sorted list makes every split peel off one card (the pivot is always the smallest), so 6 cards cost 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 comparisons, the most any order of 6 cards can cost.

claims.text: Toy quicksort with the first card as pivot, counting one comparison per other card in the group per split, takes 15 comparisons on the sorted hand 1 2 3 4 5 6.
claims.source: Builder's node script (recursive first-card-pivot quicksort, comparisons = group size - 1 per split): sorted 1..6 gives 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. Same count as the stage's ladder (sumCost over the plan in Demo.tsx). Algorithm as CLRS ch. 7 (Quicksort, first element as pivot); TheAlgorithms/Python sorts/quick_sort.py consulted only to check how the algorithm runs.

claims.text: The same toy quicksort takes 9 comparisons on the shuffled hand 3 4 1 6 2 5 (split costs 5, 1, 2, 1).
claims.source: Builder's node script: pivot 3 -> [1 2] | [4 6 5] (5); pivot 1 -> [] | [2] (1); pivot 4 -> [] | [6 5] (2); pivot 6 -> [5] | [] (1); total 9. The shuffled hand is a chosen example (not random); its cost is below the all-orders mean of 10.3 (c4).

claims.text: On the sorted hand every split leaves 0 cards on one side, because the pivot is the smallest card in its group, so each split peels off only its pivot.
claims.source: In a sorted group the first card is the smallest, so no other card is smaller: smaller side 0 cards, bigger side everything else. Group sizes go 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 with costs 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 (node, same script as c1).

claims.text: Over all 720 orders of 6 cards, no order costs more than 15 comparisons.
claims.source: Builder's node script over all 720 permutations of 1..6: maximum 15, minimum 8, total 7416 so mean 10.3 exactly. 32 of the 720 orders tie at 15 (including the reversed hand 6 5 4 3 2 1), so the sorted hand is a worst case, not the only one; the reveal says 'no order costs more' and does not say 'the only worst case'. Derivation: a split of a group of m cards costs m - 1 and leaves at most m - 1 cards, so the cost is at most (m-1) + (m-2) + ... + 1.

claims.text: For n cards the sorted-input cost is n(n - 1)/2 comparisons.
claims.source: (n - 1) + (n - 2) + ... + 1 = n(n - 1)/2; n = 6 gives 15 (node). Quicksort's worst case is Theta(n^2) when every split is maximally unbalanced: CLRS ch. 7.2 (Performance of quicksort).

claims.text: Picking the pivot at random makes this bad case very unlikely on long hands.
claims.source: Randomized quicksort runs in expected O(n log n) comparisons on every input: CLRS ch. 7.3 (A randomized version of quicksort) and 7.4 (Analysis of quicksort). For a 6-card hand the chance is not tiny; the sentence says 'long hands'.

recall.question: Quicksort with the first card as pivot is given 100 cards already in order. Roughly how many comparisons does it make?
recall.why: Each split peels off only the pivot: 99 + 98 + ... + 1 = 4,950. A balanced run would be near 700 (100 x log2 100).
